camp_ellis.what: The Army Corps of Engineers builds a jetty at the mouth of the Saco River to keep the channel open for ships. It also blocks the river's sand from reaching Camp Ellis beach.
Camp Ellis's shoreline sits about 400 feet farther out to sea than it would a century later.
The Corps adds a spur to the jetty. Engineers at the time thought sand moved north to south; later research found it moves the other way.
The Surf Street seawall (about 700 feet long) is built to hold back the sea.
A Corps study estimates the area lost about 5.9 million cubic metres of sand since 1869, but concludes the jetty wasn't the cause.
The Blizzard of '78 sets Portland's water-level record. Photos show waves bouncing off the jetty into Camp Ellis.
Maine's Sand Dune Rules ban new seawalls and limit rebuilding of houses badly damaged by storms.
The Patriots' Day storm (April) destroys another Camp Ellis house.
$45 million is announced (2022) for a 750-foot spur off the jetty to protect Camp Ellis; the Army Corps finalizes the plan in 2023.
Meanwhile, sand drifting north has built up Pine Point, enough to support about 50 more homes over 50 years.
